Campbell's Soup Cans. Andy Warhol's 1962 installation consists of 32 silk-screened canvases, each depicting a slightly different variety of Campbell's condensed soup cans at their commercial size. This work brazenly elevated mass-produced commodity packaging to fine art, crystallizing Pop Art's embrace of American consumer culture and mass reproduction as worthy subjects for artistic meditation.

First exhibited in 1962 at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles, it is now at the Museum of Modern Art and launched Warhol to fame as the iconic emblem of Pop Art. Each of the 32 canvases depicts a single Campbell's soup can rendered in commercial silk-screen printing, the same technique Warhol had learned from his graphic design background. The cans are presented frontally, isolated, and at life size, mimicking the appearance of merchandise displayed in a supermarket or on a shelf.

Warhol selected Campbell's soup as his subject partly because he ate it every day for lunch, seeing in it a democratic symbol of American convenience and mass accessibility. The work transgressed the boundary between low commercial art and high fine art, provoking outrage from critics but fascinating viewers. It pioneered Warhol's technique of using mechanical reproduction and serialization to interrogate authenticity, originality, and the artist's hand in an age of mass production.
